Correct - keep ULT steady and treat the flare with an anti-inflammatory such as colchicine.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man presents with an acute gout flare of the right knee. He has CKD stage 4 (eGFR 21 mL/min/1.73 m²), a past bleeding gastric ulcer and takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Septic arthritis has been excluded by aspiration and Gram stain.
What is the most appropriate treatment for the flare?
mcq.e: Flare options are colchicine, NSAIDs or corticosteroids; the choice depends on comorbidity. NSAIDs are contraindicated in severe CKD, peptic ulcer and anticoagulation, and colchicine must be avoided or heavily dose-reduced in severe renal impairment. Short-course oral (or intra-articular) corticosteroid is the safest choice.
w: Wrong - indomethacin is an NSAID with the same contraindications.
Correct - steroids avoid the renal, GI and bleeding risks of NSAIDs and colchicine toxicity in CKD 4.
Wrong - NSAID with CKD 4, previous bleeding ulcer and warfarin is unsafe.
Wrong - ULT does not treat a flare and should not be started at full dose, especially in CKD.
Wrong - colchicine accumulates in severe CKD, causing toxicity (myopathy, marrow suppression).

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man has had four gout flares in a year and has a tophus on the left olecranon. eGFR is 85 mL/min/1.73 m². Serum uric acid is 9.1 mg/dL. He has no drug allergies and his current flare has settled.
Which is the most appropriate way to start urate-lowering therapy?
o: Allopurinol 100 mg daily, titrate, plus colchicine
Allopurinol 600 mg daily from day one, no prophylaxis
Allopurinol only during each acute flare
Colchicine 0.5 mg daily alone as long-term therapy
Probenecid at full dose with a high-purine diet
mcq.e: Recurrent flares and tophi are indications for ULT. Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is first line: start low and go slow, titrating to a target serum urate (lecturer pearl: < 6 mg/dL, lower with tophi), with flare prophylaxis such as low-dose colchicine for the first months because rapid urate falls trigger flares.
w: Correct - start low, titrate to target, and cover with flare prophylaxis.
Wrong - high starting doses raise hypersensitivity risk and provoke flares, especially without prophylaxis.
Wrong - intermittent use causes urate swings; ULT is continuous, usually lifelong.
Wrong - colchicine prevents flares but does not lower urate or dissolve tophi.
Wrong - allopurinol is first line, and a high-purine diet works against urate lowering.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man has had recurrent painful swellings of both feet for 15 years, never treated. Foot radiographs show well-defined punched-out erosions with overhanging edges and sclerotic rims at the 1st MTP joints, with adjacent dense soft-tissue masses. Joint spaces are relatively preserved and there is no periarticular osteopenia.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges and sclerotic rims beside soft-tissue tophi, with joint space preserved until late and normal bone density, are the radiographic hallmarks of chronic tophaceous gout. RA erosions are marginal with periarticular osteopenia; PsA gives pencil-in-cup with new bone.
w: Wrong - RA shows periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions without overhanging edges or soft-tissue masses.
Correct - overhanging-edge erosions with sclerotic rims plus tophi = chronic gout.
Wrong - CPPD shows chondrocalcinosis and degenerative change, not tophaceous erosions.
Wrong - PsA shows pencil-in-cup deformity and fluffy periostitis.
Wrong - OA shows osteophytes, sclerosis and joint space loss, not punched-out erosions.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old man has a serum uric acid of 8.4 mg/dL (500 µmol/L) on a routine health screen. He has never had joint pain, has no tophi and no renal stones. eGFR is normal. BMI is 29 kg/m² and he drinks sweetened soft drinks daily.
What is the most appropriate management?
mcq.e: This is asymptomatic hyperuricaemia: gout must not be diagnosed on uric acid alone, and most hyperuricaemic people never develop gout. Management is lifestyle modification (weight loss, cutting sugar-sweetened drinks, alcohol, red meat and seafood) and addressing cardiovascular risk; ULT is not routinely indicated.
w: Wrong - uricosuric therapy is not indicated in the absence of gout.
Wrong - prophylaxis is only used to cover ULT initiation in established gout.
Wrong - febuxostat likewise is not indicated for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia.
Wrong - allopurinol is not routinely indicated without gout, stones or tophi.
Correct - asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is managed with lifestyle advice, not ULT.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old Malay man with recurrent gout and a BMI of 30 kg/m² asks for dietary advice. He currently drinks two cans of sweetened soft drink daily and eats prawns and beef several times a week.
Which dietary item should he be ENCOURAGED to include?
mcq.e: Per the Malaysian CPG Gout 2nd ed., dairy products reduce the risk of gout. Alcohol, high-fructose corn syrup (sugar-sweetened drinks), red meat and seafood (except n-3 PUFA-rich fish) increase risk. Weight reduction also lowers serum urate.
w: Correct - dairy intake is associated with a lower risk of gout.
Wrong - shellfish/seafood (other than oily n-3 fish) increases risk.
Wrong - red meat is a purine-rich risk factor.
Wrong - all alcohol raises risk, and beer is particularly purine-rich.
Wrong - fructose-sweetened drinks raise urate and gout risk.

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old woman develops a painful, warm, swollen right knee 2 days after a hip fracture operation. Temperature 37.6 °C. Aspirate: cloudy fluid, WCC 18,000/µL, Gram stain negative, with rhomboid-shaped crystals showing weak positive birefringence. Knee radiograph shows linear calcification within the menisci.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals plus chondrocalcinosis of the menisci in an elderly patient indicate acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout). It is classically provoked by surgery or acute illness and most often affects the knee. Culture should still be followed up.
w: Wrong - haemarthrosis gives blood-stained fluid, not inflammatory fluid with crystals.
Wrong - gout crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent.
Wrong - OA fluid is non-inflammatory without crystals.
Correct - rhomboid weakly positive crystals + chondrocalcinosis in an elderly knee.
Wrong - Gram stain negative, crystals present and WCC below the usual septic range (culture still awaited).

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old man has recurrent attacks of wrist and knee pain. Radiographs show calcification of the triangular fibrocartilage of the wrist and the knee menisci, with hook-like osteophytes at the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints. He has type 2 diabetes, slate-grey skin pigmentation and raised ALT.
What is the most appropriate investigation for the underlying cause?
mcq.e: Chondrocalcinosis (CPPD) in a patient under 55 should prompt a search for metabolic disease. Diabetes, skin pigmentation, abnormal LFTs and 2nd/3rd MCP hook osteophytes point to haemochromatosis, screened with ferritin and transferrin saturation. Other associations: hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphatasia, Wilson's disease.
w: Wrong - HLA-B27 relates to spondyloarthritis.
Wrong - ACE relates to sarcoidosis, not CPPD.
Correct - screens for haemochromatosis, the classic secondary cause of CPPD in a young patient.
Wrong - anti-CCP tests for RA, which does not cause chondrocalcinosis.
Wrong - urate relates to gout, and chondrocalcinosis is calcium pyrophosphate.

mcq.stem:
An 82-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 and a past bleeding peptic ulcer has an acutely swollen, warm left knee with a large effusion. Aspiration shows weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals; Gram stain is negative and WCC is 15,000/µL. She is afebrile.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
mcq.e: Acute pseudogout is treated with rest/splinting, NSAIDs or colchicine, and joint aspiration with intra-articular corticosteroid once infection is excluded. With severe CKD and a previous bleeding ulcer, NSAIDs and full-dose colchicine are unsafe, so local aspiration and steroid injection is best.
w: Wrong - urate-lowering therapy has no role; the crystals are calcium pyrophosphate.
Correct - aspiration relieves pressure and IA steroid treats inflammation with no systemic toxicity.
Wrong - colchicine accumulates in severe CKD.
Wrong - washout is for septic arthritis; infection has been excluded.
Wrong - NSAIDs are unsafe with CKD 4 and previous ulcer bleeding.

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old man has a 2-day hot, swollen right knee with rigors. Temperature 39.2 °C, HR 112/min. Aspirate is turbid: WCC 95,000/µL (92% neutrophils). Polarised microscopy shows rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals. Gram stain and culture are pending. Radiograph shows meniscal chondrocalcinosis.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: NSAIDs and a knee splint only
mcq.e: Finding crystals does not exclude infection; crystal and septic arthritis can coexist. A WCC near 100,000/µL with systemic sepsis must be treated as septic arthritis: blood cultures, empirical IV antibiotics and urgent joint washout. Intra-articular steroid would be dangerous.
w: Correct - very high WCC with sepsis is septic until proven otherwise, despite crystals.
Wrong - symptomatic treatment alone ignores probable infection.
Wrong - urate lowering has no role in CPPD or sepsis.
Wrong - discharging a septic joint risks cartilage destruction and sepsis.
Wrong - steroid injection into a possibly infected joint is dangerous.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis has painful swelling of several fingers. One finger is diffusely swollen along its whole length. Hand radiographs show asymmetrical DIP joint erosions with a 'pencil-in-cup' appearance, fluffy periosteal new bone and normal bone density.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Asymmetrical DIP disease, dactylitis, pencil-in-cup erosions and new bone formation without periarticular osteopenia are classic for psoriatic arthritis. RA spares DIPs, shows periarticular osteopenia and does not form new bone. Erosive OA gives central 'seagull' erosions.
w: Wrong - gout erosions are punched-out with overhanging edges and tophi.
Wrong - erosive OA gives central 'seagull/gull-wing' erosions and osteophytes, not pencil-in-cup with periostitis.
Wrong - reactive arthritis mainly affects lower-limb large joints after infection.
Correct - pencil-in-cup + new bone + DIP + dactylitis in a psoriasis patient.
Wrong - RA spares DIPs and shows osteopenia without new bone formation.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old woman has swollen, tender joints in both hands. Examination shows involvement of several DIP joints, nail pitting and onycholysis, and tenderness at the Achilles insertion. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are negative; CRP is raised. She has a small plaque behind one ear.
Which feature most strongly favours psoriatic arthritis over rheumatoid arthritis here?
mcq.e: DIP involvement with nail pitting/onycholysis, enthesitis and seronegativity favour PsA; RA characteristically spares DIPs. Raised CRP, morning stiffness and hand swelling occur in both inflammatory arthritides, so they do not discriminate.
w: Wrong - raised CRP occurs in both conditions.
Wrong - inflammatory stiffness is a feature of both.
Correct - DIP arthritis with nail disease is characteristic of PsA and unusual in RA.
Wrong - hand swelling occurs in both.
Wrong - RA is more common in women, so sex does not favour PsA.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man with psoriatic arthritis and extensive skin plaques has active disease despite methotrexate. He is started on ustekinumab.
Which best describes the mechanism of this drug?
o: Blocks p40 shared by IL-12 and IL-23
mcq.e: Ustekinumab is a monoclonal antibody against the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23, a biologic class separate from TNF inhibitors. The slide's 'TNF inhibitors eg: IL 12/23 inhibitors' is a slip: TNF inhibitors are adalimumab, etanercept and infliximab, while IL-12/23 and IL-17 inhibitors are distinct options in PsA.
w: Wrong - that is adalimumab/etanercept/infliximab; ustekinumab is not a TNF inhibitor.
Wrong - IL-6 receptor blockade is tocilizumab (used in RA).
Wrong - JAK inhibition is tofacitinib/baricitinib (targeted synthetic DMARDs).
Wrong - B-cell depletion is rituximab.
Correct - ustekinumab targets the p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old woman with long-standing untreated psoriasis has progressively shortened fingers. Several digits can be passively pulled out and pushed back in with skin folding. Radiographs show severe osteolysis of the phalanges with pencil-in-cup changes.
What is the name of this pattern?
mcq.e: Arthritis mutilans is the most severe, destructive pattern of psoriatic arthritis: osteolysis of the phalanges and IPJs produces unstable, shortened 'telescoping' (opera-glass) digits. Swan-neck and boutonnière are tendon-imbalance deformities seen mainly in RA.
w: Wrong - boutonnière is PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension from central slip rupture.
Wrong - Charcot joints occur with neuropathy (e.g. diabetic foot), not psoriatic phalangeal osteolysis.
Correct - osteolysis with telescoping digits is arthritis mutilans.
Wrong - swan-neck is PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion, not telescoping.
Wrong - erosive OA has central erosions but does not cause telescoping.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man from Sabah has a 5-month history of a swollen, mildly warm right knee, low-grade evening fevers, night sweats and 6 kg weight loss. The quadriceps are wasted and there is a 15° flexion contracture. Radiograph shows juxta-articular osteopenia and erosions at the joint margins, with the joint space largely preserved.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: An insidious chronic monoarthritis of a weight-bearing joint with constitutional symptoms and the Phemister triad (juxta-articular osteopenia, peripheral erosions, gradual joint space narrowing) is classic TB arthritis. Pyogenic arthritis is acute and destroys cartilage within days, so joint space is lost early.
w: Wrong - pyogenic arthritis presents acutely over days with early joint space loss.
Wrong - gout gives episodic acute flares and punched-out erosions, not constant fevers and osteopenia.
Wrong - RA is a symmetrical polyarthritis; isolated monoarthritis with weight loss and fevers points to TB.
Wrong - PVNS causes recurrent haemarthrosis without constitutional symptoms.
Correct - insidious monoarthritis + evening fever/weight loss + Phemister features.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old woman has a chronic swollen left knee for 6 months, with weight loss. Synovial fluid is turbid and xanthochromic with WCC 18,000/µL and low glucose. Acid-fast bacilli smear and Gram stain are negative. IGRA is positive. Chest X-ray is clear.
Which investigation offers the highest diagnostic yield?
o: Sputum AFB smear on three days
MRI of the left knee with contrast
mcq.e: Synovial fluid AFB smears are frequently negative in TB arthritis. Synovial biopsy gives the best yield: histology shows epithelioid granulomas with caseating necrosis, and tissue culture/PCR confirms M. tuberculosis with drug sensitivities. IGRA and Mantoux show TB infection but cannot prove active joint disease.
w: Wrong - the chest X-ray is clear; sputum is unlikely to be positive and does not prove joint TB.
Wrong - smears are often negative; repeating adds little.
Wrong - like IGRA, it shows infection, not active TB arthritis.
Correct - tissue histology (caseating granuloma) plus culture has the highest yield.
Wrong - MRI shows synovitis and erosions but cannot give a microbiological or histological diagnosis.

mcq.stem:
Two patients have a painful swollen knee. Patient A has a 3-day history, fever 39.5 °C and severe pain. Patient B has a 4-month history, evening fevers and weight loss.
Which radiographic feature most favours tuberculous over pyogenic arthritis?
o: Rapid, early loss of joint space
mcq.e: TB pannus erodes the peripheral, non-weight-bearing margins and lacks the proteolytic enzymes of pyogenic infection, so cartilage and joint space are relatively preserved early (gradual narrowing) despite marked juxta-articular osteopenia. Pyogenic infection destroys cartilage within days and may heal by bony ankylosis; TB typically heals by fibrous ankylosis.
w: Wrong - TB causes marked juxta-articular osteopenia.
Correct - relative preservation of joint space with marginal erosions is typical of TB (Phemister).
Wrong - bony ankylosis is a pyogenic outcome; TB tends to fibrous ankylosis.
Wrong - rapid joint space loss is typical of pyogenic infection.
Wrong - gas suggests gas-forming pyogenic organisms, not TB.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man has culture-confirmed, drug-sensitive tuberculous arthritis of the right hip. Joint cartilage is largely preserved and there is no abscess. He weighs 60 kg and has normal liver function.
What is the most appropriate definitive treatment, per the lecture slides?
mcq.e: Bone and joint TB is treated medically with anti-tuberculous therapy: a 2-month intensive phase of ethambutol, isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide (2EHRZ), then a 4–7 month maintenance phase of isoniazid and rifampicin (4–7HR), for 6–9 months total. Surgery is reserved for abscess, severe destruction, deformity, drug resistance or atypical mycobacteria.
w: Correct - standard ATT regimen for bone and joint TB per the slides.
Wrong - surgery never replaces ATT; synovectomy alone leaves active infection.
Wrong - isoniazid monotherapy treats latent TB only and breeds resistance in active disease.
Wrong - cloxacillin treats staphylococcal pyogenic arthritis, not TB.
Wrong - arthroplasty is reserved for destroyed joints after disease control, not first line.
